title: Fan Curve Explorer
creator: Twin City Fan
subject: fan curve
stall region
brake horsepower
non-overloading power curve

description: Plotly chart of two illustrative fans' pressure and BHP curves with a six-question check that asks the learner to differentiate stall-region from stable operating points and overloading from non-overloading power curves.
rights: Copyright 2026 Twin City Fan. All rights reserved.

educational.audience: Adult professional development: application engineers, sales staff, representatives and specifying engineers
educational.topic: Fan curves, stall region and power curves
learningObjectives: Differentiate stable from stall-region operating points by locating each point relative to the pressure-curve peak
Differentiate overloading from non-overloading power curves by reading the shape of the BHP curve
Read the maximum BHP of a non-overloading curve as the motor size that cannot be overloaded at that speed

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Hover-to-read exploration followed by committed answers with immediate feedback
keyQuestions: Is 3,000 CFM on Curve A in the stall region?
Is 9,000 CFM on Curve A in the stall region?
Is 6,000 CFM on Curve B in the stall region?
Is 11,000 CFM on Curve B in the stall region?
Which curve has a non-overloading power curve?
What is the highest BHP anywhere on Curve A?
commonMisconceptions: Any point the pressure curve passes through is a safe operating point, including points left of the peak
A fan's BHP always rises with airflow
The highest-pressure point is the best place to select a fan
assessmentOpportunities: Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt; question 6 is correct within 0.1 of 9.5 BHP

dataProvenance: Illustrative curves shaped after typical backward inclined (Curve A) and forward curved (Curve B) centrifugal fan behavior; not Twin City Fan published ratings.
